steps.title: Two nouns, no word for "of"
body: English says "the man's house" or "the house of the man". Arabic just puts the two nouns next to each other: بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ — literally "house-of the-man". No possessive word, no extra particle.

The two nouns don't behave the same way. The first (مُضَاف) takes whatever case its role in the larger sentence needs, but it drops its own الـ and tanwīn — it can never carry either, even though the phrase as a whole ends up definite. The second noun (مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ) is always genitive, keeps its الـ, and is what makes the whole phrase definite: بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ is "the man's house", definite, even though بَيْتُ itself has no الـ.
This is called إِضَافَة (iḍāfa) — "the backbone of Arabic phrasing", because it's how Arabic expresses almost every possessive relationship: a country's capital, a book's title, a student's pen.

steps.title: House, man, pen, student
steps.intro: Read the bare phrase first, then the two full sentences that use it. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Which noun loses الـ?
steps.prompt: Why doesn't بَابُ carry الـ, even though "the door of the house" is definite?

options.label: The first noun in an iḍāfa never takes الـ — definiteness comes from the second noun
بَاب is always indefinite and can never take الـ
It's a typo — it should be الْبَابُ

steps.explanation: بَابُ (مُضَاف) drops الـ and tanwīn no matter what; الْبَيْتِ (مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ) keeps الـ and carries the definiteness for the whole phrase.

steps.title: Spot the genitive
steps.prompt: What case is الرَّجُلِ in, and why?

options.label: Genitive — the second noun in an iḍāfa is always genitive
Nominative — it's the subject of the sentence
Accusative — it's the object of a verb

steps.explanation: الرَّجُلِ ends ـِ because it's مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ — the second noun of an iḍāfa is genitive regardless of what role the phrase as a whole plays in the sentence.

steps.title: A different pair
steps.prompt: Which word is مُضَاف (the possessed thing, no الـ of its own)?
steps.explanation: قَلَمُ carries no الـ or tanwīn of its own, exactly like بَيْتُ and بَابُ before it — the same iḍāfa pattern, a different pair of nouns.

steps.title: You can read Arabic possession
steps.message: You've seen iḍāfa three times now — بَابُ الْبَيْتِ، بَيْتُ الرَّجُلِ، قَلَمُ الطَّالِبِ — always the same shape: the first noun bare, the second definite and genitive. This one pattern covers most of how Arabic expresses possession.
